svg.text: Where the Dust Goes: Four Fates
Once airborne, dust leaves the air by a small number of routes. All four matter, and only one of them is routinely measured.
1 Back to the ground, then up again
The largest single fate, and the only one that repeats.
Settles under gravity (dry deposition) or is washed out by rain (wet deposition).
Where the surface is vegetated, it enters the soil and largely stays there.
Where the surface is a road, a pavement or a roof, a tyre or a gust lifts it again.
The same mass of dust can be raised and dropped many times before it leaves.
A street swept at noon can look grey again by evening.
No new construction is needed for that to happen.
2 Into secondary pollution
Dust is not only a mass of particles. It is also a reaction surface.
Sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and organic gases oxidise in the air.
They combine with ammonia to form sulphate, nitrate and ammonium salts.
Those salts stay airborne for days and make up a large share of PM2.5 mass.
Airborne dust offers an alkaline surface on which some conversions run faster.
The outcome is not dust plus haze. It is one combined problem.
Reducing one input slows the other at the same time.
3 Into the lungs
The route that decides how much the other three actually matter.
PM10 lodges in the larger airways; PM2.5 crosses the lung barrier into the blood.
From there it reaches major organs rather than staying in the chest.
Associated with heart and respiratory disease, lung cancer and stroke.
In 2015 the IARC concluded that particulate matter in outdoor air causes lung
cancer. Children in high-PM2.5 areas show slower lung growth.
The fraction that matters most is the fraction you cannot see.
4 Into water, soil, plants and materials
The slow, quiet fate that outlasts the dust episode itself.
Deposits into water bodies, where it affects water quality and clarity.
Settles on leaves; the metals and organic compounds in it can affect growth.
Soils building facades, windows and solar panels.
Reduces visibility, and shifts the local heat balance: dark particles warm,
while sulphate and nitrate particles cool.
Dust does not stay in the city that produced it.
Three of the four routes are not exits
Settled dust is a reservoir that waits for the next vehicle, the next gust or the next dry spell. Secondary
chemistry keeps converting gases into new particles. Inhaled dust does not disappear either — the body clears it
over time, and the material returns to surfaces and to soil.
The practical consequence: control has to work on the surface, not only in the air.
Suppressing a plume in flight is one half of the job. Removing the material that can be lifted again is the other.
